# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

Researchers (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Priyanka Raghunathan → [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work"; the fine-tuning run is the author's.
- Tobias Brandt → [HN] the genomics comment (bursty pipeline, "about 8 different steps", "We need to reserve the $MAX requirements for each").
- Ana Lucía Ferreira → [HN] the student's "so I overestimate" on simulation time; the queue wait for a big request is the author's.
- Kwabena Owusu → author's invention, filling a gap: an ML engineer whose sizes come from past runs on a dashboard, so the problem is not a chorus (against on Importance and Current solution).
- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention: a chipped (rather_not_say) story at a quant fund, GUESSED by code.
- Rafael Moreno → author's invention: a vague, habitual story (GUESSED), echoing [HN] "everyone over-requests by two to three times".
- Ingrid Haugen → author's invention: a gate No (writing up, no jobs that week).
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention: a gate No (away at a conference).
- Yusuf Demir → [HN] "snooping on sumbit scripts ... many of them are egregiously bad": a copied script holding eight GPUs.
- Claire Dubois-Martin → author's invention, filling a gap: a licensed binary with no source code, so the tested condition fails ('no').
- Hiroshi Takeda → [HN] "at least for everyone else, I'd would prefer tuning my own usage myself": he profiles a test run (Current solution mostly works; Adoption friction no).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → [HN] "you lose days of work"; the walltime limit and the group allocation are the author's.
- Diego Castañeda → [HN] the student's PDE simulation ("If I'm running a PDE simulation, and I allocate n machines I want to use all of them"); he keeps his margin (Adoption friction probably not).

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.
- Leilani Kahale → [HN] "In many places the cost of the HPC hardware isn't passed onto them": a grant-funded university cluster that does not measure the waste (dont_know) and has no line for a monthly fee.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

founder.order_why: It runs from naming the project and the market, through the context and its look-back window, to the problem beliefs and stories, then who asks and who gets the link, which is how I'd explain Expanse to someone.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the same question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'). If 5 only reads back what I typed on 3, it is a check, but it looks like the same question asked again.
founder.missing: Nothing asked what a wrong guess costs a researcher: a job killed mid-run and days of work lost when they under-request, or GPUs held and never used when they over-request by two to three times. That cost is the core of my problem, and the problem step only asks how many guess, how often, what else is hard and how they cope today.

PRIMARY.order_why: Screen 4 asks what I'd most like made easier before screen 5 has me recall how my last guess actually went, so I'm picking a priority before I've thought through the job where it went wrong; swapped, it would follow how I'd tell it.
PRIMARY.missing: What the bad guess cost me: whether the job was killed mid-run for too little memory or time, how many hours or days of work I lost and had to resubmit, and on the other side how long I waited in the queue for over-requesting. Also how I come up with the numbers now, whether from past runs, a profiling run or just padding the max.

screens.why5: My whole point is that everyone over-requests two to three times, yet the line puts 'requested too much' with the jobs where today's way worked, so the screen has drifted from what I typed.
screens.why7: The line sits under a shortfall rung ('requested too much'), which the card forbids, so my core problem counts against the belief; the rungs mix two measures, wasted compute and failed runs; and the bar on the list names 'Padded it a little; it ran, a little idle', a rung that is not on the final list.
screens.instead: Think of the last job you submitted. How much of what you requested did it use? Sized about right, ran to the end · ┄ line ┄ · Ran, but a third of the request sat idle · Ran, but half or more sat idle · Failed mid-run, then ran on resubmit · Never ran to the end; then I can't recall

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs right before the study goes out to researchers, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs video, voice, typing, credits and text-message delivery into one block, and it says Keel records the 'voice' while the interviewer is on video with a face, so I had to read it twice to know what I was locking.
screens.why3: Which interviewer my researchers hear is my call to make, and I can make it by tapping play on each.
screens.why4: Two names with a 5-second sample each is a complete choice, but nothing says how Daphne and Saskia differ (tone, accent, look), so I can't choose without playing both.
screens.why5: It keeps my people as researchers and adds nothing to my product or roles.
screens.instead: Who should ask researchers your questions? Daphne (picked for you; calm, US accent ▶ 5 s) or Saskia (brisker, UK accent ▶ 5 s). The face and voice you lock are recorded once for this project for 400 credits.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks my researchers, it is obvious I next pick how they answer, just before the study is sent.
screens.why2: Each option says plainly what the researcher sees and does (a video interviewer speaking aloud, or reading and tapping), so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I know how my researchers work, mostly at a terminal between job submissions, so I can judge whether they would rather read and tap than talk to a video interviewer.
screens.why4: The three options are complete and distinct, but the third calls the second one *text* instead of *Read and tap*, which makes me check that they are the same thing.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes my study or my words; it only asks how researchers and ML engineers will answer.
screens.instead: Keep the screen, but in the third option say 'they pick Daphne or Read and tap when they open the link'.

screens.why1: After choosing how researchers answer, deciding who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending, and I know whose names I'd send it to: the researchers on the clusters we've talked to.
screens.why2: It is clear on first reading, but the second option switches from my voice ('I send') to Keel's ('Pick a list... and you send them'), so I have to re-read who is doing what.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm sending to researchers I know by name, to a list, or posting in a cluster's user channel, because that is my own outreach.
screens.why4: The three ways I could reach researchers (named people, a found list, one open link posted in a Slack or HPC user list) are distinct, and together they cover how I'd actually send it.
screens.why5: My pick, 'People I know by name', each with their own link, is shown as I chose it, and nothing about Expanse leaks into the choice.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (I send each their own link) / People I found with Keel (I pick a list from Contacts; Keel makes a link for each and I send them) / A group, one open link (I post it where they already are, e.g. the cluster's user Slack; each signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is stated with '4 counted' beside it, but it names only Frequency when Importance and Current solution are equally short, and the '5 needed' that decides it sits only on the cards, not by the verdict.
screens.why_b2: The tally (1 holding, 3 too few to call, 7 answered) and each card's bar read plainly, but the kicker's '4 TO 7 COUNTED' takes a second look, and the count line just repeats the tally, so nothing on the page says why only 4 of 7 were counted.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution are word for word what I checked, and Prevalence and Frequency are my submit-time guessing in my window and my working days.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need one more counted researcher on three cards, but the page never says to send the study to more researchers or why three of seven dropped out (gate No, guessed), so I am left inferring the next step.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible everywhere, too-few is said plainly, and Prevalence is shown as 'at the bar' at 6 of 7 rather than called strong.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of 4 beliefs (Frequency, Importance, Current solution) have 4 counted of 5 needed; 3 of your 7 were not counted (2 had no jobs that week, 1 too vague), so send it to a few more researchers who submitted jobs this week; Prevalence holds, just, at 6 of 7.

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar', so I know it held and by exactly what number.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 6 cells for me and 1 against, out of 7 on a 0-to-7 axis, with my bar marked at 6, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card names Prevalence and my 'at least 8 in 10', but the belief has become 'guessed a job's resource request', which is the circumstance I typed, not my problem (over-requesting and wasting the cluster, or the job dying mid-run); it also drops my 'SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs' qualifier.
screens.why_b4: 'How often, and whether it matters, are the next two cards' points me onward, but it never says what a Yes to 'did you guess' tells me about the waste I sell against, so I am not told what to do with this result.
screens.why_b5: The small group is said ('a lean, not a call'), but 'Holding up' on a question every submitter answers Yes to overstates support for my problem; even Kwabena, whose sizes come from past runs on a dashboard, counts for me.
screens.instead: Ask and state the cost, not the act: 'In the last 5 working days, did you pad a job's request and leave GPUs idle, or have one killed mid-run for asking too little?', and say that a Yes to merely guessing proves little.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats both.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts working days out of 5 over 4 people with my 3-to-5 band marked, but it draws a 0 tick no one could answer, and the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' sits beside four cells all for me while the verdict is still no call, so I had to look twice to see the floor of 5, not the bar, is what holds it back.
screens.why_b3: 'Guess a job's resource request before submitting it on 3 to 5 working days out of 5' is my circumstance in my trade's words, with the range I set.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it does not say that one more counted researcher would decide it, or that the four so far all sit inside my range.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (6 answered, 4 counted), each uncounted answer is named with its reason, and the small group is called a lean, not a call.
screens.instead: Too few to call: all 4 counted researchers guessed on 3 to 5 days of 5 (middle answer 4), but 5 are needed; get one more clear answer before you lean on this.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, 4 counted of the 5 needed, and the So line repeats both.
screens.why_b2: The caption makes clear that the bars count 8 picks from 4 people and that my item got 3, but 'your bar · 4 of 5' on the strip reads at first like a tally rather than the bar of 4 'for' needed once 5 are counted, so I had to look twice.
screens.why_b3: The card's title is Importance and its belief line is word for word the one I checked, with my own item 'Guessing memory, GPUs and run time' marked as the problem I named.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' tells me not to act, but it does not say that 3 of my 4 counted researchers already put it in their two, or that one more counted answer would settle it.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible throughout, the two uncounted people are named with the reason, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps 3 of 4 from being oversold.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of the 4 counted put guessing memory, GPUs and run time in their two; one more counted researcher who picks it would make 4 of 5 and hold it, so get one more answer before you lean on this.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats both, so I know why there's no call: one short of the floor.
screens.why_b2: The rungs, their counts and my line are plain, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' with a marker at 4 over 3 for, 1 against and a ghost cell takes a second look before I see it means 4 of the 5 needed would have to land below the line.
screens.why_b3: The belief line is word for word the one I checked, and the bar names my rung 'Padded it a little; it ran, a little idle' exactly as it stands on the list.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't say that one more counted answer would decide it, or that 3 of the 4 already lean my way, two of them by doubling everything to be safe.
screens.why_b5: n is visible (6 answered, 4 counted), each person left out is named with the reason, and the screen calls it 'a small group: a lean, not a call' rather than claiming a hold.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', but the screen never says how many of the 4 put guessing in their two, so I can't see how close the belief came to the bar of 2 in 3.
screens.why_b3: Importance and the belief line are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies 'get more answers', but nothing says what one ML engineer losing the day to data movement and library conflicts means for Expanse, or that Current solution never got its why asked.

screens.why_b6: Kwabena's line, that sizes copied from last week's runs are fine and the real pain is data staging and software environments, is a competitor-for-attention I hadn't typed, but it is a single quote standing alone with no theme beside it.

screens.why1: As the first screen it obviously checks whether I'm the kind of person the study wants: someone running on a big shared GPU cluster.
screens.why2: Cluster, jobs and GPUs are everyday words for me, so I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know roughly how big our cluster is, so I can answer from what I do, though someone on a cluster near 100 GPUs might have to think for a second.
screens.why4: A screener's yes or no is complete and distinct, and §5 says the gate has no escape, so none is missing.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 100-GPU segment and gives away nothing about any product or plan.
screens.why6: It is short, one question and easy to answer on one hearing, though §17's screener form (the stem, then 'Yes or no.') would sound more natural than 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.'
screens.instead: In the last week, did you submit a job to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes cluster with 100 or more GPUs? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I'm on a 100-plus GPU cluster, asking about my last few days of submitting jobs is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Resource request and submitting a job are everyday words for anyone writing sbatch scripts or pod specs, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I put in my last job's request this week, so I can answer from my own work.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to the gate.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but the founder's problem was the cost of guessing wrong (a job killed mid-run, days lost, the cluster wasted), and this asks only that I guessed, which is the circumstance.
screens.why6: It is one short question with 'Yes or no' at the end, easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: The gate asks the circumstance every researcher in the segment is in, since every SLURM or Kubernetes job needs its memory, GPUs and time guessed, so everyone says Yes, No has nobody, and the founder's band can never be refuted.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did a job of yours get killed or wasted because you guessed its memory, GPUs or run time wrong? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to guessing a resource request this week, it makes sense to ask how many days that happened on.
screens.why2: Resource request and submitting a job are how I talk about SLURM every day, so I can answer it on first read, though I'd say estimate more often than guess.
screens.why3: I know which days this week I submitted jobs and had to set memory, GPUs and wall time, so I can count them.
screens.why4: The buttons 1 to 5 cover every working day without overlap, and I can't recall is the one escape and sits apart.
screens.why5: It asks about my own submissions in my own trade's terms, with nothing about a product or the founder's roles.
screens.why6: It is one short question with the unit said once and a number from 1 to 5, so I can hold it after one hearing.
screens.why7: Every option counts days of the 5-day window, from 1 to the window's count, with no 0, no bands and the cant_recall escape alone, so the founder's range can be read against them.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether and how often I guessed a job's resource request, it makes sense to ask how that compares with the other things that are a pain when I run jobs.
screens.why2: Memory, GPUs, run time, allocation and getting software working are everyday words for anyone submitting to SLURM, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: Every row is something I deal with myself in my own submissions, so I can answer from my own last runs without guessing.
screens.why4: The set is complete and distinct, but *Running out of the group's allocation* is a bad outcome rather than a task, so it reads backwards after *made easier*, unlike the other four.
screens.why5: The guessing of memory, GPUs and run time before submitting stays as the founder put it, and nothing about a product or tool reaches me.
screens.why6: Five options plus one escape say well, but *guessing memory, GPUs and run time* puts a comma list inside the semicolon list, so it is a mouthful to hold by ear.
screens.why7: The founder's own row is there, not first, beside four rivals with *None of these* at the first ask, so the belief can be supported or refuted, but two rules bend: the own row holds a list inside it, and the allocation row is an outcome rather than a task on the one measure.
screens.instead: Think of your last run of jobs on the cluster. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Getting software working on the cluster · Setting a job's resource request · Waiting for a job to start · Keeping within the group's allocation · Moving data on and off the cluster · None of these

screens.why1: After picking which part I'd most like made easier, asking how my last guess at memory, time and GPUs actually went is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Memory, time and GPUs, padding a request, a job dying and being resubmitted: that's exactly how I'd talk about it.
screens.why3: I sized my last job myself and know whether it ran, sat idle or got killed for under-requesting.
screens.why4: 'Copied an old script and hoped' is a method with no outcome and overlaps the others, since a copied script can also have run as planned. The answer I most fear, the job dying late and losing days of work, has no rung of its own beyond 'died and was resubmitted'.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or the founder's terms reaches me; it is about my own last submission.
screens.why6: Every option is two clauses joined by a comma when spoken ('padded it a little, it ran, a little idle'), which is a mouthful to hold five times over.
screens.why7: The measure (did the job run without wasting the cluster), the working first rung and the escape I can't recall all fit, but every rung carries a method the card forbids, and the last rung is a method rather than the job failing outright, so it cannot count for or against the belief.
screens.instead: Think of your last job. How did its resource request work out? Ran to the end, little sat idle · Ran, but a fair share sat idle · Ran, but most of it sat idle · Died once, resubmitted bigger · Died late, days of work lost — or I can't recall
